title: Fatherhood & Sacrifice
description: Dante learns to care for Mel, navigates loss of his university plans, and the novel's theme of male nurturing.
content_html:
The Demands of Real Fatherhood

Once Emma has gone and the reality of the situation becomes clear, Dante must simply get on with it. He has a baby daughter who is approximately ten months old, who cannot walk, who needs feeding, changing, comforting, and constant attention. He has no experience. He has no instruction manual. He has only his father Tyler — himself a man who raised two sons alone after the death of their mother — and whatever he can work out for himself.

Blackman presents the early stages of Dante's fatherhood without romanticisation. He is exhausted. He gets things wrong. He does not know how to read Mel's different cries. He does not know what she needs at two in the morning when she screams. The novel's portrait of parenting is specific and physical: nappies, milk, sleep deprivation, and the particular difficulty of managing a ten-month-old who is old enough to have strong preferences and reactions but too young to communicate them in words.

Key Fact

Mel is approximately ten months old. She arrived in a pushchair, not as a newborn. The specific demands Dante faces — a baby who is mobile, reactive, and demanding but unable to speak — are central to Blackman's portrait of involuntary fatherhood.

Sacrifice: What Dante Gives Up

The central sacrifice at the heart of Dante's storyline is his university place. He had worked towards studying journalism — a specific, carefully chosen ambition. A-level results day, which was supposed to be the beginning of his future, became the day his future was replaced by a different one.

Blackman takes care to show that Dante does not make this sacrifice quickly or easily. He wrestles with it. He considers possible routes — could he still go? Could someone else look after Mel? — before arriving at the reality that there is no adequate solution that does not involve him taking primary responsibility for his daughter's care. The journalism degree is not deferred. It is, for now, gone.

The sacrifice has symbolic weight. Journalism is about telling the truth, bearing witness, giving a voice to those who are not heard. Dante is now living a story he cannot yet tell. His sacrifice is not just material (the degree, the career) but also about identity: the version of himself he was going to become has been interrupted.

Part of what makes the novel's resolution satisfying is that Dante's sacrifice is not presented as permanent destruction. By the end, he has not recovered his journalism degree — but he has come to see Mel not as the thing that destroyed his future but as something integral to who he is. The novel does not pretend the sacrifice was easy or small. It does not resolve the loss. But it offers Dante a future that includes both Mel and a version of the self he was building before she arrived.

Tyler as a Model: The Widower Father

Tyler Bridgeman's parenting is the template Dante has grown up with. Tyler is a widower: his wife — the boys' mother — died of cancer. He raised Dante and Adam alone, not because he was abandoned or because a partnership broke down, but because he was bereaved. His emotional landscape has been shaped by grief that he has never fully processed. He is stoic, practical, and present — but not emotionally expressive. He provides. He does not open up.

When Mel arrives, Tyler's response is instructive. He does not condemn Dante. He does not perform shock or outrage. He assesses the practical reality and helps. This is the only mode of fatherhood he knows: stoic acceptance and practical action. For Dante, Tyler's model is both a gift and a limitation. It gives him a foundation — he has seen what it looks like for a man to take full parental responsibility without complaint. But it does not give him a template for emotional expressiveness or vulnerability.

Key Fact

The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler is a widower, not a man whose partner left him. His emotional guardedness is rooted in unprocessed grief — a man who has buried loss under duty and practicality. His parenting is an act of love expressed through action rather than words.

Blackman's Argument About Masculinity

The novel's title — Boys Don't Cry — is a phrase used to police male emotional expression. Boys are told, from childhood, that vulnerability is weakness, that tears are failure, that masculinity means stoicism and endurance. The novel challenges this at every level.

Dante's journey into fatherhood is partly a journey into the emotional life he has been taught to suppress. Caring for Mel requires him to be attentive, patient, and emotionally present in ways that the traditional male scripts around him do not support. He cannot be stoic with a ten-month-old who needs comfort. He must actually show up emotionally. This is Blackman's central argument: the capacity to nurture is not gendered. Boys can cry. Men can care.

Both brothers are, in different ways, under pressure to conform to a version of masculinity that does not fit them. Dante is expected to be free of parental responsibility at seventeen — fatherhood is not in the script. Adam is expected to be heterosexual — his sexuality is not in the script. Both are living outside the expectations placed on them as young men. Blackman uses the dual-narration structure to show these pressures operating simultaneously, and the climax — when the two storylines converge in violence — is the moment at which the pressure of social expectation becomes literally lethal.

Growing into Fatherhood

Over the course of the novel, Dante's relationship with Mel changes. The initial shock and helplessness give way, slowly, to competence. He learns what she needs. He learns her patterns. He learns to read her differently at different times of day. And with competence comes something else: attachment.

Mel is not an obstacle in Dante's story. She is not something he merely tolerates while waiting for his real life to begin. Blackman charts the transition from Dante caring for Mel because he has no choice to Dante caring for Mel because he loves her. This transition is the emotional spine of his storyline — and by the novel's end, it is clear that whatever future Dante builds, Mel is part of it.
exam_tip_html: When writing about the theme of fatherhood, make sure you demonstrate awareness of Blackman's specific choices: Dante plans to study journalism (not a generic university course), Mel is approximately ten months old (not a newborn), and Tyler is a widower (not an abandoned partner). These specific details matter to examiners. They also signal that you have read carefully rather than relying on a generic overview.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dante's sacrifice is specific: he gives up a planned journalism degree to care for Mel, who is approximately ten months old and arrived in a pushchair.
  • Tyler models stoic, practical fatherhood rooted in grief — he is a widower whose wife died of cancer, not a man whose partner left him.
  • The title 'Boys Don't Cry' is a social script that the novel systematically dismantles — Dante's journey into fatherhood requires emotional presence, not stoicism.
  • Both brothers are under pressure to conform to masculine expectations that do not fit them — the dual narration shows these pressures operating simultaneously.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present the theme of sacrifice through Dante's experience of fatherhood? You should consider the context in which the novel was written.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of sacrifice. Discusses: journalism degree as specific ambition sacrificed; the transition from shock to competence to attachment; the novel's refusal to sentimentalise the sacrifice while also showing that it produces growth. Context: masculinity, social expectations of teenage fatherhood, Blackman's challenge to gender norms.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman use Tyler Bridgeman to explore the costs and values of a particular model of fatherhood?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of Tyler as a model. Discusses: his stoicism, his practicality, his steadiness — and his emotional limitation. The roots of his behaviour in unprocessed grief (wife died of cancer, not abandonment). How Dante learns from Tyler's model but must also exceed it by developing emotional expressiveness that Tyler cannot offer. Context: grief, masculinity, fatherhood in British culture.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

Context: changing expectations of masculinity in early 21st-century Britain, Blackman's feminist and humanist aims.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Blackman charts Dante's growing attachment to Mel over the course of the novel.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of the transition from obligation to love. Discusses: initial shock and incompetence, gradual acquisition of parenting skills, the shift from caring because he has no choice to caring because he is attached. How Blackman avoids sentimentality while making the emotional development convincing. Mel's specific age (ten months) as a narrative choice that gives her a developing personality.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited discussion.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman use the parallel stories of Dante and Adam to explore the pressures placed on young men by society's expectations?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive structural analysis. Discusses: both brothers living outside social expectations (unexpected fatherhood; open homosexuality); the dual narration showing these pressures operating simultaneously; the way each brother's story challenges a different aspect of traditional masculinity; the convergence of the two storylines in the attack. Context: masculinity norms, homophobia, social conformity.
Top band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant contrasts.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.

knowledge_checks.q: What was Dante planning to study at university before Mel arrived?
What does the novel's title 'Boys Don't Cry' refer to?
options: A song playing at the party where Adam is attacked
A social script that tells men they must not show emotional vulnerability
Adam's refusal to cry after the homophobic attack
Tyler's inability to grieve for his wife

knowledge_checks.q: Tyler's emotional guardedness is rooted in _____.
options: his anger at the boys' mother for leaving
his disappointment in Dante's teenage fatherhood
unprocessed grief after his wife died of cancer

knowledge_checks.q: How old is Mel when she arrives with Emma at the start of the novel? (Complete the answer: _____)
Match each idea to the character it applies to:
right: Sacrifices his journalism degree to care for Mel
Models stoic, practical fatherhood rooted in grief as a widower
Are placed under pressure by social expectations that do not fit their lives

flashcard_questions.q: What is the significance of Dante's specific ambition to study journalism?
flashcard_questions.a: Journalism is about truth, voice, and bearing witness — Dante's sacrifice is not just a degree but a chosen identity as a truth-teller.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Boys Don't Cry' mean as a social script?
flashcard_questions.a: A cultural instruction that tells men they must not show emotional vulnerability — the novel systematically challenges this.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Tyler have emotional limitations as a father?
flashcard_questions.a: His wife died of cancer — he is a widower who buried grief under stoicism and duty. His guardedness comes from loss, not abandonment.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Dante's fatherhood require a different kind of masculinity than Tyler's model?
flashcard_questions.a: Caring for Mel requires emotional presence and vulnerability — Tyler's stoic, practical model is not enough. Dante must learn to express feeling.

flashcard_questions.q: What transition does Dante go through in his relationship with Mel?
flashcard_questions.a: From caring for her because he has no choice to genuinely loving and being attached to her — competence precedes connection.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Mel approximately ten months old, rather than a newborn, significant to the novel?
flashcard_questions.a: She is old enough to have reactions, preferences, and a developing personality — Dante must engage with her as a person, not just as a helpless infant.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the parallel between Dante and Adam support the novel's theme?
flashcard_questions.a: Both are living outside social expectations — unexpected fatherhood and open homosexuality. Both are pressured to conform to masculine norms that do not fit them.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Blackman avoid sentimentalising Dante's growth into fatherhood?
flashcard_questions.a: She shows the exhaustion, mistakes, and physical demands of caring for a ten-month-old before she shows the attachment — the love is earned, not given.

glossary_terms.definition: Making something seem more beautiful, heroic, or romantic than it actually is. Blackman avoids romanticising Dante's early fatherhood.
Enduring difficulty without complaint or emotional display. Tyler models stoic fatherhood — but the novel challenges this as insufficient.
The qualities and behaviours associated with being a man in a particular culture. Boys Don't Cry examines and challenges traditional masculine norms.
A deep emotional bond between a parent and child, forming gradually through sustained care. Dante's attachment to Mel develops over the course of the novel.
Giving up something of value for something else. Dante sacrifices his journalism degree and planned future to care for Mel.
